title_home: How to create a company in South Korea?

roadmap.title: Roadmap to create your startup in Korea
roadmap.subtitle: Step-by-step guide for foreign entrepreneurs

step1.title: Get the right visa
step1.description: Before anything else you need legal permission to run a business in Korea. Here are the main visa options available to foreign founders.
step1.details:
Choosing your visa is the very first strategic decision of your project: it determines how quickly you can get set up, the steps you'll need to complete, and how much freedom you'll have to grow your business.

Four main visas are available to foreign founders in Korea. Find the situation below that best matches your project to discover the most suitable path, compare the options in detail, then follow the typical journey to the D-8-4 visa.

tabs.title: Which visa matches your profile?
tabs.subtitle: Four main paths lead to founding a company in Korea. Find the one that matches your situation and compare its requirements, duration, and benefits.

items.name: Tech Investor Visa (OASIS)
items.summary: This is the standard path for foreign founders. Your application is assessed by KISED using a points-based scale (degrees, experience, intellectual property, funding). Once approved, you register your company and then obtain the visa.
items.idealFor: You have a well-developed project: a solid business plan, a patent, a prototype, or recognized entrepreneurial experience.
advantages: Valid for 1 year, renewable for up to 2 years after confirmation
Full official recognition and access to KISED support and public funding programs
requirements: OASIS points-based assessment (degree, experience, patents, funding)
Company registered in Korea (Chusik or Yuhan Hoesa)
Capital deposited in a dedicated bank account
items.watchOut: The OASIS assessment process can take several months.

items.name: Streamlined path (since November 2024)
items.summary: Thanks to a direct recommendation from your program, your application is processed faster with fewer supporting documents required. This is the fastest path for founders who already have institutional backing.
items.idealFor: You've completed a recognized accelerator program (K-Startup Grand Challenge, TIPS, Born2Global...).
advantages: Accelerated processing with reduced supporting documentation
requirements: Direct recommendation from an approved partner program (K-Startup Grand Challenge, TIPS...)
Simplified application, without a full points-based assessment
items.watchOut: Reserved for founders already selected by a recognized partner program.

items.name: Startup preparation visa
items.summary: This temporary long-term stay visa lets you legally remain in Korea to finalize your business plan and put together your OASIS application, before transitioning to the D-8-4.
items.idealFor: You want to explore the Korean market and prepare your application calmly before committing.
advantages: Lets you prepare your OASIS application and company registration without time pressure
requirements: No company registration required to obtain it
items.watchOut: Does not allow paid commercial activity - preparation only.

items.name: Points-based talent visa
items.summary: Based on a points scale (age, degree, income, Korean proficiency...), this visa is not tied to a specific company. It offers more freedom but does not replace standard company registration.
items.idealFor: You have a senior profile (advanced degree, professional experience, solid income) and want to keep your activity flexible.
advantages: 3 years, renewable, can lead to permanent residency (F-5)
Great flexibility: change activity, combine statuses, and easier access to permanent residency
requirements: Minimum score on the points scale (age, degree, experience, income, Korean proficiency)
Proof of degrees and professional experience
No mandatory link to a specific company
items.watchOut: Does not include startup-specific benefits (KISED programs and funding).

specialCase.title: Are you a student in Korea (D-2 visa)?
specialCase.description: If your project was born during your studies, many universities - including PNU - have an industry-university cooperation foundation that can support you in moving from student status to D-8-4 founder status, without leaving the country.

timeline.title: The path to the D-8-4 visa
timeline.subtitle: The standard path, via KISED's OASIS program, in seven steps.

items.title: Prepare your application
items.description: Gather your degrees, resume, business plan, and proof of experience or patents, translated and apostilled.

items.title: Submission on the OASIS platform
items.description: Submit your application online on KISED's platform for assessment under the points-based scale.

items.title: Assessment and interview
items.description: KISED reviews your application. An interview may be arranged depending on your profile and industry.

items.title: Recommendation letter
items.description: If approved, KISED issues a recommendation letter required for your visa application.

items.title: Company registration
items.description: With the KISED recommendation letter in hand, you can finalize your company's legal registration with the commercial court - share capital, articles of incorporation, filing the application.

items.title: Submitting the visa application
items.description: File your application with the Korean consulate if you are abroad, or with the local immigration office for a change of status.

items.title: Getting your visa and ARC card
items.description: Once your D-8-4 visa is approved, apply for your Alien Registration Card (ARC) within 90 days of entering Korea.

checklist.title: What not to forget
checklist.subtitle: Four essential points to plan for, whichever visa you obtain.

items.title: Private insurance
items.description: Take out private health insurance covering at least 100 million KRW before submitting your application.

items.title: Clean criminal record
items.description: Provide a clean criminal record extract, apostilled or legalized, along with an official translation.

items.title: Resident card (ARC)
items.description: Apply for your Alien Registration Card within 90 days of arrival: it's essential for opening a bank account or signing up for a phone plan.

items.title: Annual renewal
items.description: Plan ahead for your visa renewal: the company's actual activity, revenue, and jobs created are reviewed against KISED's criteria.

step2.title: Choose a legal structure
step2.description: Corporation LLC or sole proprietorship each has different implications in terms of liability taxation and funding.
step2.details:
Your company's legal status determines your level of financial liability, your tax regime, your credibility with banks and investors, and how burdensome your day-to-day administration will be. Changing it after registration remains possible, but proves costly and time-consuming - better to choose well from the start.

Two statuses account for the vast majority of foreign startup formations in Korea: the Chusik Hoesa (joint-stock company) and the Yuhan Hoesa (limited liability company). Compare them below based on your project, then review the key points common to both statuses to plan for before registration.

tabs.title: Which structure for your company?
tabs.subtitle: The two most common statuses for foreign founders in Korea. Compare them to choose the one that best fits your project.

items.name: Chusik Hoesa
items.summary: The most recognized structure for startups planning to raise funding. It offers more flexibility for bringing in investors and is favored by Korean venture capital funds.
items.idealFor: Startups aiming for fundraising or rapid growth with multiple co-founders.
advantages: Easier share issuance to bring in new investors
The structure best recognized by VCs, accelerators, and public programs
Stronger institutional image with banks and partners
requirements: One shareholder and one director are enough to get started
Share capital deposited in a dedicated bank account before registration
Roles and ownership percentages defined in the articles of incorporation before registration
items.watchOut: More formal governance: general meetings, a shareholder register, and minutes must be kept up to date. A statutory auditor becomes mandatory if capital exceeds 1 billion KRW.

items.name: Yuhan Hoesa
items.summary: A structure that's simpler to set up and run day-to-day, well suited if you're starting out solo or with a small team without an immediate need to bring in outside investors.
items.idealFor: Solo founders or small teams, service or consulting businesses.
advantages: Simplified incorporation and day-to-day management formalities
No requirement for a statutory auditor
requirements: A single member is enough, 100% foreign capital allowed
Share capital deposited in a dedicated bank account before registration
Articles of incorporation drafted in accordance with Korean law
items.watchOut: Less suited if you plan to open your capital to investors: conversion into a Chusik Hoesa remains possible but must be planned ahead.

checklist.title: Key points to know
checklist.subtitle: Four principles that apply regardless of the structure you choose.

items.title: 100% foreign capital
items.description: Korea allows foreign founders to hold the entirety of their company's capital, with no local partner required.

items.title: A single shareholder is enough
items.description: No requirement to partner with anyone: one person alone can found and hold the entirety of a Chusik Hoesa or a Yuhan Hoesa.

items.title: Statutory auditor
items.description: For a Chusik Hoesa, a statutory auditor becomes mandatory as soon as capital exceeds 1 billion KRW.

items.title: Registration cost
items.description: Budget for roughly 0.4% of registered capital, with a minimum of 112,500 KRW, excluding attorney fees.

step3.title: Secure a business address
step3.description: A registered Korean address is required to establish a company. Options include virtual offices or government backed startup centers.
step3.details:
This address is not a mere administrative detail: recorded in the articles of incorporation filed with the commercial court, it becomes your 본점 (official head office) and determines where your company may legally operate. Changing it after registration requires updating the articles of incorporation and completing new registry formalities - so it's best to make the right choice from the start.

Four main options are available to foreign founders, from virtual offices to personal addresses. Compare them below based on cost, what's included, and the founder profile they suit, then review the points to check before signing a lease or accepting a spot in an incubator.

comparison.title: Which address for your head office?
comparison.subtitle: Four main options are available to foreign founders: compare their cost, what's included, and the profile they suit.

items.name: Virtual office
items.includes: Registrable business address, mail reception and scanning, occasional access to meeting rooms.
items.idealFor: Founders based outside Korea or remote teams who only need a legal address.
items.watchOut: The lease agreement provided must explicitly authorize commercial use and company registration: ask for a template already accepted by the registration office before signing.

items.name: Co-working space
items.cost: from ≈ 120,000 KRW / month for a dedicated desk
items.includes: Dedicated desk or private office, meeting rooms, networking events, registrable address on dedicated plans.
items.idealFor: Small teams who want a real workspace without committing to a traditional commercial lease.
items.watchOut: Only "private office" or "business address" plans allow registration: a simple open-space membership is generally not accepted by the commercial registry.

items.name: Public startup center
items.cost: Free to very low cost, by selection
items.includes: Workspace, support with registration and visa, mentoring, and networking with investors, through structures such as the Global Startup Center or KISED incubation centers.
items.idealFor: Foreign founders in the founding phase, eligible for government support programs.
items.watchOut: Limited spots awarded by application: allow several weeks of selection time before getting an address usable for registration.

items.name: Personal address
items.cost: 0 KRW if you already live there
items.includes: Your lease or property title serves directly as proof of head office, at no extra cost.
items.idealFor: Unregulated activities, with no public reception, inventory, or on-site team.
items.watchOut: Many condominium regulations prohibit commercial use of a residential unit, and some activities require commercial zoning: check both points before choosing this option.

checklist.title: Four points to check before signing
checklist.subtitle: Whichever type of address you choose, these elements affect your registration and the rest of your setup.

items.title: Proof of address is mandatory
items.description: Whatever you choose, a lease agreement or property title - in your name or the future company's name - is required in the registration file submitted to the commercial court.

items.title: Your address becomes the official 본점
items.description: It appears in the articles of incorporation (정관) filed at registration: it becomes your legal head office and determines, among other things, your tax jurisdiction and competent court.

items.title: Changing address comes at a cost
items.description: Moving after registration requires an amendment to the articles of incorporation (본점이전) and a new entry in the commercial registry, with additional fees and procedures: better to plan for a stable address from the outset.

items.title: Watch out for zoning
items.description: Some regulated activities (food service, healthcare professions...) require a specific commercial zone: check that your address is compatible with your activity before signing a lease or accepting a spot in an incubator.

step4.title: Register your startup
step4.description: The official process including required documents registration offices and expected timelines.
step4.details:
This step is the administrative core of your project: without registration, you cannot open a corporate bank account, hire staff, or legally issue invoices. The procedure involves several different authorities - the bank, KOTRA, the commercial court - and each document obtained serves as supporting evidence for the next step.

Three phases follow one another, from depositing capital to filing the articles of incorporation with the court. Follow them in order below, prepare the required documents in advance, and find out what you receive at the end of the process.

phases.title: Three phases to register your company
phases.subtitle: Each phase produces a document required for the next phase. Follow them in order.

items.title: Investment notification and capital deposit
items.description: Before any other step, notify your foreign direct investment to KOTRA or a bank licensed for foreign exchange, then transfer the declared capital to a temporary foreign-currency account.
documents: Deposit balance certificate confirming the capital paid in

items.title: Company name reservation
items.description: Check availability and reserve your company name with the court registry. Names must comply with Korean naming conventions and industry classifications - a step that often creates delays without professional support.
documents: Company name compliant with Korean industry classifications

items.title: Filing the articles of incorporation and application with the court
items.description: Submit the full application to the commercial court. If an agent files the application on your behalf, powers of attorney must be provided in two copies.
documents: Copy of the articles of incorporation
Apostilled passports of directors and shareholders
Notarized power of attorney (two copies if filed by an agent)

documents.title: Two types of documents to plan for
documents.subtitle: Some documents are obtained in Korea over the course of the process, while others must be prepared in advance in your home country.

columns.title: Obtained in Korea during the process
To prepare in your home country
items: Articles of incorporation, drafted under Korean law
Passports of directors and shareholders, apostilled
Notarized power of attorney if an agent files the application
columns.note: All foreign documents (articles of incorporation, power of attorney, resolutions) require notarization followed by an apostille or consular legalization, as well as an official Korean translation.

outcome.title: What you receive at the end of the process
outcome.subtitle: Two official documents that establish your company's legal existence - and that you'll use immediately in the next step.

items.name: Corporate registration number
items.description: Issued by the commercial court via the Internet Registry Office, this number officially identifies your company and certifies its legal existence.

items.name: Corporate seal certificate
items.description: The 인감 (corporate seal) and its official certificate are used to authenticate the company's legal and banking documents.

step5.title: Open a bank account
step5.description: Often the most challenging step for foreigners. Here are the banks that are foreigner friendly the paperwork to prepare and tips to avoid rejection.
step5.details:
Opening a corporate bank account turns the capital held in the temporary account into actual company cash flow. Korean banks apply strict anti-money-laundering checks - an in-branch visit is often required, along with a substantial set of documents - and then impose deadlines you must meet to finalize your foreign-invested company status with KOTRA, with penalties if you miss them.

Some Korean banks are markedly more experienced with foreign founders' applications than others: compare them below before choosing your branch, then follow the timeline of deadlines to meet once your account is open.

banks.title: Which bank for your corporate account?
banks.subtitle: All major Korean banks can open a corporate account, but some are markedly more experienced with foreign founders' applications.

items.name: KEB Hana Bank
items.description: Considered the most accessible bank for foreigners: mobile app available in English and dedicated "Global" branches for foreign residents and foreign-invested companies.
points: App and customer service in English

items.name: Woori Bank
items.description: Has a department dedicated to foreign-invested companies and a very large branch network, useful if your head office is located outside Seoul.

items.name: Shinhan Bank
items.description: Its "Shinhan Global" network is present in several home countries of foreign investors, which can make it easier to get in touch even before you arrive in Korea.

items.name: KB Kookmin Bank
items.description: Korea's leading retail bank by number of branches, with a department specialized in supporting foreign direct investment (FDI) companies.

timeline.title: Deadlines to meet after depositing capital
timeline.subtitle: Once the corporate account is open, several deadlines follow one another - some with direct consequences if missed.

items.title: Capital already deposited in a temporary account
items.description: When you notified your investment, your capital was paid into a temporary account opened in the future representative's name - this is the capital that will be transferred to the new corporate account.

items.title: Opening the corporate account
items.description: Allow about 4 weeks: present the articles of incorporation, the certificate of incorporation, the corporate seal certificate, and the passports and ARCs of the directors. Documents issued outside Korea generally must be apostilled and translated into Korean.

items.title: End of anti-money-laundering restrictions
items.description: During the first 20 business days, transfer limits are reduced and opening a second account at another bank is blocked - a standard control measure used by Korean banks.

items.title: FDI registration to finalize with KOTRA
items.description: The foreign currency deposit certificate issued by your bank must be submitted to KOTRA to obtain your foreign-invested company certificate (외국인투자기업등록증), within a maximum of 60 days after the capital is paid in.

step6.title: Register for taxes
step6.description: Overview of the Korean tax system for startups including VAT and corporate tax.
step6.details:
Without a business registration certificate (사업자등록증), your company can neither issue tax invoices nor fully operate its corporate bank account - it's the last administrative gate before normal operations. Foreign-invested companies must also appoint a Korean tax agent, responsible for preparing and filing all their returns in Korean with the NTS.

Once these formalities are complete, your company enters the standard tax regime: progressive corporate income tax, 10% VAT, and, under certain conditions, a significant tax reduction for young companies. Find the details of each point below.

formalities.title: Two formalities before filing
formalities.subtitle: These two steps determine your ability to legally invoice and report your income in Korea.

columns.title: Business registration certificate (사업자등록증)
columns.description: Apply via Hometax or with the local tax office within 20 days of starting operations. Without this certificate, you cannot issue tax invoices (세금계산서) or fully unlock your corporate bank account.
items: Certificate of incorporation from the commercial court
Proof of lease for your head office

columns.title: Mandatory tax agent (회계대리인)
columns.description: Foreign-invested companies must appoint a national tax agent (회계대리인), a Korean accounting firm that becomes your official point of contact with the NTS.
items: Prepares and files your VAT and corporate income tax returns
All returns are drafted in Korean
Generally billed monthly or quarterly, in addition to your accounting fees

brackets.title: Corporate income tax brackets (법인세)
brackets.subtitle: The applicable rate depends on your company's annual taxable profit, plus a local surtax equal to 10% of the national rate.
brackets.note: Brackets in effect since January 1, 2026 - each bracket rose by one point compared to the previous scale.

items.range: Up to 200 million KRW in taxable profit
items.note: Almost all early-stage startups remain in this bracket.

stats.title: Three figures to know
stats.subtitle: Beyond the corporate tax brackets, three elements shape your day-to-day taxation.

items.label: VAT (부가가치세)
items.description: Standard rate applied to most goods and services, to be filed quarterly with the NTS.

items.label: Startup tax reduction
items.description: During the first 5 years, depending on your head office's location - capped at a cumulative reduction of 500 million KRW.

items.label: Annual filing
items.description: Deadline to file your corporate income tax return after your fiscal year closes.

step7.title: Find funding
step7.description: Korea offers generous public programs grants accelerators and venture capital firms that support foreign founders.
step7.details:
Between accelerator grants, R&D funding, and preferential public loans, the Korean government injects several billion KRW into its startup ecosystem every year. But most of this funding flows through selective programs: a company's age, industry, and foreign-investor status determine access to each of them.

Here are three entry points designed for foreign founders, followed by the criteria to check before putting together your application.

pathways.title: Three entry points to fund your startup
pathways.subtitle: Each program targets a different profile - choose the one that matches your stage, your industry, and your existing investors.

items.name: K-Startup Grand Challenge
items.description: The Korean government's flagship program for startups founded by non-Koreans: about a hundred teams selected each edition, including a track reserved for foreign students. Winners receive on average 50 million KRW (up to 80 million) for product development, localization, and marketing, with 8 months of support through to COMEUP's Demo Day.
points: Non-Korean startup less than 7 years old (10 years for deep tech)
Priority sectors: AI, biotech, fintech, mobility, energy
Privileged access to the D-8-4S visa for winners

items.name: TIPS
items.description: An R&D and commercialization grant that can exceed 100 million KRW per company, within a national pool raised to 5 billion KRW. Access isn't direct: you need a recommendation from an approved TIPS operator - an investment fund or accelerator partnered with the program.
points: Startup less than 7 years old, recommended by an approved TIPS operator
For foreign startups: at least USD 1 million already raised from foreign investors
Can be combined with other sector-specific grants (food tech, deep tech...)

items.name: KOSME loans (정책자금)
items.description: Public funds (정책자금) from the Korea SMEs and Startups Agency finance cash flow, investment, and exports at below-market rates. For 2026, the national pool exceeds 4,400 billion KRW, geared toward manufacturing, productive investment, and international expansion.
points: Company registered in Korea, generally for less than 7 years
Apply through the new "Policy Fund Navigator," which directs you to the right program based on your profile
Can be combined with grants, contrary to popular belief

checklist.title: Four criteria before applying
checklist.subtitle: These programs share common eligibility conditions - worth planning for before starting an application.

items.title: Registered foreign investor (FDI) status
items.description: Most of these programs - and the tax benefits that come with them - assume your company has foreign-invested company (FDI) status, registered with KOTRA.

items.title: Less than 7 years old (10 for deep tech)
items.description: Your company's age is calculated from its official registration date, not from when the project began. The clock starts at the previous step.

items.title: An eligible industry
items.description: AI, biotech, fintech, mobility, energy... Most programs for foreign founders target priority sectors defined each year by the Ministry of SMEs and Startups (MSS).

items.title: An operator or investor who recommends you
items.description: For TIPS in particular, you don't apply alone: an approved investment fund or accelerator must first select you and recommend you to the program.

step8.title: Get insured
step8.description: Once you start hiring you must enroll in Korea’s mandatory insurance programs covering health pension and unemployment.
step8.details:
Enrollment in the 4 major social insurances (4대보험) must be completed within 14 days of hiring for health insurance, and by the 15th of the following month at the latest for the other three programs - missing this exposes you to retroactive contribution claims and, for some programs, penalties. Rates were also revised upward on January 1, 2026, with the pension contribution increase set to continue every year through 2033.

Here's how each of the four contributions is split between employer and employee, followed by three labor law benchmarks to know before your first hire.

contributions.title: The 4 mandatory social insurances (4대보험)
contributions.subtitle: Each one is split differently between employer and employee - factor this into your total labor cost calculation.

items.name: National Pension (국민연금)
items.note: Rate raised from 9% to 9.5% on January 1, 2026, as part of a reform that will increase it by 0.5 points each year until it reaches 13% in 2033.

items.name: National Health Insurance (국민건강보험)
items.note: Raised from 7.09% to 7.19% on January 1, 2026, plus an additional surcharge for long-term care insurance (장기요양보험), also split equally.

items.name: Employment Insurance (고용보험)
items.note: The base rate (unemployment benefits) is split equally. The employer alone additionally pays 0.25% to 0.85%, depending on company size, for skills development (고용안정·직업능력개발사업).

items.name: Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance (산재보험)
items.note: Fully paid by the employer. The base rate varies widely by industry and risk level, with three additional flat-rate contributions: commuting accidents (0.06%), wage guarantee (0.06%, excluding the public sector), and asbestos compensation (0.006%, companies with 20 or more employees).

facts.title: Three benchmarks for your first hire
facts.subtitle: Beyond social insurance contributions, these three rules apply from your very first employee.

items.label: Minimum hourly wage (2026)
items.description: About 2,156,880 KRW per month based on 209 hours, up 2.9% from 2025. Applies to all employees, regardless of nationality.

items.label: Severance pay (퇴직금)
items.description: Average wage × 30 days × (days worked ÷ 365), owed to any employee with at least one year of continuous service, regardless of the reason for departure.

items.label: Social security agreements
items.description: Depending on the nationality and residency status of your foreign employees, these agreements may exempt them from certain pension or unemployment contributions in Korea.
